metadata.title: Engagement, achievement, and teacher classroom practices in mathematics: Insights from TIMSS 2011 and PISA 2012

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2011 and PISA 2012 microdata and estimates parameters at the student level. For TIMSS 2011, descriptive and inferential analyses are weighted using the student sampling weight totwgt, and replicate weights are handled via jackknife replication weights; for PISA 2012, analyses use the student sampling weight W_FSTUWT and balanced repeated replication (BRR) weights. The authors restrict PISA inferential analyses to the subset of students who received the rotated questionnaire forms containing the engagement and teacher-practice items, consistent with PISA rotation design guidance. Although the paper does not use ML algorithms, it explicitly applies complex-survey weighting and replication to obtain population-representative estimates and correct variance estimation under the ILSA sampling design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study focuses on eighth graders in TIMSS 2011 and uses mathematics achievement outcomes derived from TIMSS 2011 continuous mathematics scores (five PVs) converted to achievement-level outcomes for model convergence. For PISA 2012, the study uses 15-year-old students’ mathematics literacy outcomes and restricts analyses to the subset of students who completed the rotated questionnaire forms containing the engagement and teacher-classroom-practice items (about one-third of the sampled students), treating the resulting missingness as missing at random due to rotation design. For TIMSS 2011 teacher-reported classroom practices, countries with low teacher response (Australia) are handled via multiple imputation (m=5) for the teacher-practice variables, while other TIMSS countries with <5% missingness use listwise deletion. In all cases, the final SEM/path models are estimated at the student unit of analysis using robust WLS (WLSMV) for ordinal observed indicators.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (eighth graders; engagement in mathematics; teacher-reported practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM/CFA + path analysis (WLSMV); fit indices reported as RMSEA and CFI for measurement/structural models (e.g., RMSEA 0.07–0.05; CFI 0.97–0.98 across countries). Path coefficients: teacher practices mostly null; SES positive (β=0.06 Singapore; β=0.16 Finland; β=0.15 Australia; β=0.10 Romania).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge along with gender and socioeconomic status to model students’ latent interest in mathematics, finding that teacher-reported classroom practices showed little to no association with interest across countries while socioeconomic status was a consistent positive predictor. This indicates that, in these TIMSS contexts, engagement-related attitudes are more strongly patterned by students’ home resources than by the measured frequency of instructional practices, suggesting that engagement interventions may need stronger equity components alongside classroom practice improvements.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (eighth graders; engagement in mathematics; teacher-reported practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): challenge → self-concept significant in Australia (β=0.11) only; gender → self-concept positive in all four countries (β=0.11 Singapore; β=0.16 Finland; β=0.17 Australia; β=0.06 Romania); SES → self-concept positive across countries (β=0.17 Singapore; β=0.24 Finland; β=0.21 Australia; β=0.28 Romania). R2 for self-concept: 0.04–0.09 across countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge plus gender and socioeconomic status to predict students’ latent self-concept in mathematics, finding that teacher-reported challenge had a limited positive association only in Australia while gender and socioeconomic status were consistently and positively related to self-concept across all four countries. This indicates that strengthening students’ perceived competence may require addressing socioeconomic disparities and gender-linked differences, while the measured teacher-practice composites alone may not be sufficient to shift self-concept broadly.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (eighth graders; engagement in mathematics; teacher-reported practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): teacher practices mostly null; challenge → future utility beliefs not significant in most countries; gender → future utility beliefs significant in Australia (β=0.11) only; SES → future utility beliefs positive in Singapore (β=0.05), Finland (β=0.19), Australia (β=0.12), and Romania (β=0.04). R2 for future utility beliefs: 0.01–0.05 across countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge along with gender and socioeconomic status to predict future utility beliefs, finding that teacher-reported instructional practices were largely unrelated to future utility while socioeconomic status showed a consistent positive association across countries. This indicates that policies aiming to improve students’ long-run value beliefs may need to prioritize socioeconomic supports and targeted engagement strategies rather than relying solely on the frequency of generic classroom practices.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics (eighth graders; engagement in mathematics; teacher-reported practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): challenge → math achievement significant in Finland (β=0.12), Australia (β=0.15), and Romania (β=0.12) but not in Singapore; structure and support not significant; SES → math achievement strong positive across countries (β=0.37 Singapore; β=0.32 Finland; β=0.43 Australia; β=0.50 Romania). R2 for math achievement: 0.12–0.28 across countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2011 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge plus gender and socioeconomic status to predict mathematics achievement levels, finding that socioeconomic status was the strongest and most consistent predictor while teacher-reported challenge showed small but significant positive associations in Finland, Australia, and Romania. This indicates that improving achievement may require both equity-oriented supports (given the dominant SES gradient) and careful calibration of challenging instruction, while generic structure/support practices may not translate into measurable achievement gains in these cross-sectional models.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; engagement in mathematics; student-reported teacher practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): structure → interest significant in Singapore (β=0.11), Finland (β=0.20), Australia (β=0.18) but null in Romania; support → interest significant in Singapore (β=0.27), Finland (β=0.21), Australia (β=0.26) but null in Romania; challenge → interest significant only in Romania (β=0.19); SES → interest negative in Singapore (β=-0.05) and positive in Finland (β=0.13) with null in Australia and Romania; gender effects small (e.g., Finland β=0.11; Australia β=0.12). R2 for interest: 0.03–0.21 across countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged student-reported teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge along with gender and socioeconomic status to predict students’ latent interest, finding that structure and support were generally positively associated with interest in Singapore, Finland, and Australia but not in Romania, while challenge related to interest only in Romania. This indicates that classroom practice effects on engagement are context-dependent and that student perceptions of supportive/structured instruction may be a more actionable lever than generic challenge frequency, though cross-country differences imply the need for localized implementation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; engagement in mathematics; student-reported teacher practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): structure → self-concept significant in Finland (β=0.25) and Australia (β=0.14) but null in Singapore and Romania; support → self-concept positive across all countries (Singapore β=0.16; Finland β=0.12; Australia β=0.18; Romania β=0.24); challenge → self-concept negative in Finland (β=-0.13) and null elsewhere except Romania positive (β=0.09) and Singapore null; gender → self-concept positive in Singapore (β=0.07), Finland (β=0.19), Australia (β=0.20), Romania (β=0.07); SES → self-concept positive across countries (Singapore β=0.17; Finland β=0.19; Australia β=0.10; Romania β=0.13). R2 for self-concept: 0.09–0.17.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged student-reported teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge plus gender and socioeconomic status to predict students’ latent self-concept, finding that teacher support was a consistently positive predictor across all four countries while challenge showed heterogeneous effects (negative in Finland, positive in Romania, and mostly null elsewhere). This indicates that policies promoting supportive instructional practices may be broadly effective for strengthening students’ perceived competence, whereas “more challenge” is not uniformly beneficial and should be implemented with attention to appropriateness and context.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; engagement in mathematics; student-reported teacher practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): structure → future utility beliefs significant in Singapore (β=0.15), Finland (β=0.23), Australia (β=0.19) but null in Romania; support → future utility beliefs positive in Singapore (β=0.19), Finland (β=0.16), Australia (β=0.19) and null in Romania; challenge → future utility beliefs significant only in Romania (β=0.19); SES → future utility beliefs negative in Singapore (β=-0.10) and positive in Finland (β=0.16) with null in Australia and negative in Romania (β=-0.05). R2 for future utility beliefs: 0.03–0.15.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged student-reported teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge along with gender and socioeconomic status to predict future utility beliefs, finding that structure and support were generally positively associated with future value beliefs in Singapore, Finland, and Australia but not in Romania, while challenge related positively only in Romania. This indicates that improving students’ long-run value beliefs may depend on perceived instructional organization and support, and that generic challenge-oriented reforms may require careful adaptation to local student reference frames.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; engagement in mathematics; student-reported teacher practices)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path coefficients (standardized): structure → math achievement significant in Finland (β=0.16) and Australia (β=0.09) but null in Singapore and Romania; support → math achievement significant in Australia (β=0.08) only; challenge → math achievement negative across countries (Singapore β=-0.14; Finland β=-0.28; Australia β=-0.16; Romania β=-0.16); SES → math achievement positive across all countries (Singapore β=0.40; Finland β=0.29; Australia β=0.35; Romania β=0.42); gender → math achievement small positive in Finland (β=0.07), Australia (β=0.07), Romania (β=0.06) and null in Singapore. R2 for math achievement: 0.14–0.24.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged student-reported teacher classroom structure, support, and challenge plus gender and socioeconomic status to predict mathematics achievement levels, finding that socioeconomic status was consistently positively associated with achievement while challenge showed a consistently negative association across all four countries. This indicates that reforms emphasizing “challenging instruction” may backfire if challenge is perceived as miscalibrated or if student perceptions reflect relative standing, so instructional quality should be operationalized as appropriately challenging with adequate support rather than challenge frequency alone.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2011 (Grade 8 mathematics) and PISA 2012 (15-year-old mathematics) data from four focal countries—Singapore, Finland, Australia, and Romania—to examine how emotional/cognitive engagement (interest, self-concept, future utility beliefs) relates to mathematics achievement and teacher classroom practices. Teacher practices are measured as composites of structure, support, and challenge, reported by teachers in TIMSS 2011 and by students in PISA 2012. The models are estimated with CFA and path analysis using robust WLSMV for ordinal indicators, applying student sampling weights (totwgt in TIMSS; W_FSTUWT in PISA) and corresponding replicate weights (jackknife in TIMSS; BRR in PISA). Across both datasets, socioeconomic status is a strong predictor of engagement and achievement (e.g., SES → achievement β≈0.32–0.50 in TIMSS; β≈0.29–0.42 in PISA), while teacher-practice effects are heterogeneous: support is consistently positive for self-concept in PISA, whereas challenge is negatively associated with achievement in PISA. The findings are correlational due to cross-sectional secondary analysis and may reflect reverse causation and measurement differences between teacher- and student-reported practices.
